origin_region: Yunnan (Menghai, Lincang, Yiwu and Pu'er origins)
cultivar: Seed-grown old-tree Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica) maocha
processing: Old-tree maocha is fermented in small batches, often off the ground in bamboo baskets or wooden boxes rather than in a floor pile, and usually to a lighter or medium degree to preserve the material's sweetness and aftertaste; then dried, rested and pressed into cakes.
harvest_season: Mostly spring old-tree maocha, with autumn leaf in cheaper lots; sold by production year and origin.
appearance_dry: A dark-brown cake of large, thick, intact leaves with long stems and fat golden buds, looser and more irregular than a factory cake.
appearance_liquor: Deep, bright red-brown, glossy and very clear.
appearance_wet: Thick, elastic, whole dark leaves that spring back when pressed, unlike the soft mush of plantation shu.
taste_profile: Ripe tea with the texture of good raw material: thick and oily, dates and honey rather than earth, a clean woody depth, a sweetness that returns in the throat, a mild bitterness in lighter fermentations and a long session of twelve or more steeps.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice with boiling water. Boiling water throughout and long late steeps; the thick leaf keeps giving. Porcelain shows the clarity, clay adds roundness.

vintage_note: Sold by production year, origin and tree class, as cakes of 200–357 g from boutique makers, and the category only dates from around 2008–2012, when old-tree maocha became expensive enough that fermenting it was a statement; everything on sale is therefore 1–15 years old, with most of it 2015–2025. Lightly fermented lots need 2–4 years to settle and then improve for a decade, keeping some raw-tea brightness; fully fermented ones drink well at once. Kunming-dry storage is the norm for this tea and suits its clarity. Expect prices several times those of factory shu, and expect many 'gushu shu' cakes to be ordinary plantation leaf with a premium wrapper, because fermentation hides a great deal.
description:
Gushu shu is ripe pu-erh made from old-tree maocha, the same expensive material that goes into boutique raw cakes, and it is the premium end of a category that was built on cheap plantation leaf. It only became a thing around the late 2000s, when a few producers decided that the thickness and aftertaste of old-tree leaf would survive fermentation and be worth the gamble; the better examples prove them right.

The fermentation is different as well as the leaf: small batches, often off the ground in bamboo baskets or wooden boxes where the heat and moisture can be controlled, and frequently a lighter or medium degree that stops short of the full, dark Menghai style so the material keeps its sweetness and returning aftertaste. The tea is then dried, rested and pressed loosely.

In the cup, good gushu shu is thick and oily like a raw old-tree tea but with ripe flavours: dates, honey and clean wood instead of earth, a sweetness that climbs in the throat, a mild bitterness in the lighter fermentations and a session that runs twelve steeps or more without turning thin. The wet leaf is the tell, thick and elastic rather than mushy. Boiling water, two rinses and long late steeps.

It is sold by production year, origin and tree class at several times the price of factory shu, and because fermentation hides a lot, it is also where plantation leaf most easily passes for old-tree. Judge the texture, the length of the session and the springiness of the wet leaf rather than the wrapper, and treat a cheap 'gushu shu' as a well-made ordinary shu. Lightly fermented lots deserve a few years before judgement.

If you have liked ripe pu-erh only as a comfort drink, a good gushu shu is the one that shows it can be a serious tea.
